Sensor Calibration, Fusion, and Measurement Uncertainty

bayesAgriFlow

Source: vignettes/v38-sensor-fusion-and-uncertainty.Rmd
v38-sensor-fusion-and-uncertainty.Rmd

Purpose

Remote-sensing measurements can be precise without being accurate for a biological target, and multiple platforms can disagree systematically. Version 1.3.0 therefore separates calibration, fusion, and measurement-error propagation. This distinction prevents a common shortcut in which every sensor column is treated as error-free truth.

1. Calibration versus prediction

Calibration estimates the relationship between a sensor proxy and a reference measurement. Prediction then applies that relationship to new observations. A good calibration fit does not itself prove transportability to another date, sensor, cultivar, or site.

d <- bayes_teaching_data("rs_calibration")
cal <- bayes_rs_calibrate(d, "ground_biomass", "uav_biomass", draws = 1000)
print(cal)
head(predict(cal, d))

Interpretation checklist

  • Keep calibration and external validation distinct.
  • Report the range of reference values used.
  • Avoid extrapolating far beyond the calibration range.

2. Approximate calibration draws

bayes_rs_calibrate() fits a transparent Gaussian linear calibration and draws coefficients from the estimated sampling covariance. It is a lightweight teaching and preprocessing utility, not a replacement for a full posterior hierarchical calibration when both sensor and reference are uncertain.

cal$diagnostics
str(cal$coefficient_draws, max.level = 1)

Interpretation checklist

  • Call the coefficient draws approximate.
  • Use the full measurement-error model when reference uncertainty matters.
  • Inspect residuals before applying the calibration.

3. Grouped calibration

Sensors may behave differently by platform, campaign, or calibration panel. A grouping variable can fit separate linear calibrations. Separate models should only be used when each group has enough reference support.

cal_g <- bayes_rs_calibrate(
  d, "ground_biomass", "uav_biomass", group = "campaign", draws = 500
)
cal_g$diagnostics

Interpretation checklist

  • Do not create tiny calibration groups.
  • Report whether group-specific calibration was planned.
  • Consider a hierarchical model when partial pooling is preferable.

4. Known predictor uncertainty

The main modeling layer can accept standard-error columns for selected sensor predictors. Internally, the brms route uses latent mi() formulations so known predictor uncertainty is propagated instead of pretending the observed predictor is exact.

u <- bayes_teaching_data("uav")
des_me <- bayes_rs_model(
  u, "biomass", predictors = c("ndvi", "canopy_height"),
  predictor_sd = c(ndvi = "ndvi_se"),
  spatial = FALSE
)
bayes_plan(des_me)

Interpretation checklist

  • Standard errors must be positive and scientifically justified.
  • Known sensor uncertainty is not the same as estimated residual variance.
  • Do not fabricate standard errors simply to activate the feature.

5. Measurement error changes the estimand

When a predictor is error-prone, the model targets the latent predictor relationship rather than the naive relationship with the observed noisy value. This can alter effect magnitude and uncertainty. The distinction should be stated in reports.

Interpretation checklist

  • Name the latent scientific quantity.
  • State where the measurement-error SD came from.
  • Perform sensitivity analysis if the uncertainty estimate is itself uncertain.

6. Multiple error-prone features

More than one remote-sensing predictor can carry known uncertainty. Each error-prone predictor receives an auxiliary latent-variable equation. This is powerful but computationally heavier and can become weakly identified when predictors are highly correlated.

des_me2 <- bayes_rs_model(
  u, "biomass", predictors = c("ndvi", "ndre"),
  predictor_sd = c(ndvi = "ndvi_se", ndre = "ndre_se"),
  spatial = FALSE
)

Interpretation checklist

  • Check collinearity among latent predictors.
  • Use informative priors when scientifically justified.
  • Validate the measurement model with simulation when possible.

7. Multi-sensor fusion is explicit

bayes_rs_fusion() accepts a named list of source-specific predictors. In 1.3.0, fusion means that these source features enter one auditable response model. The package does not silently claim a latent common-sensor process that the data cannot identify.

f <- bayes_teaching_data("sensor_fusion")
des_f <- bayes_rs_fusion(
  f, "biomass",
  sources = list(
    uav = c("uav_ndvi", "height"),
    satellite = "sat_ndvi",
    proximal = "proximal_index"
  ),
  x_coord = "x", y_coord = "y"
)
des_f$model_options$fusion_sources

Interpretation checklist

  • Name every source.
  • Do not treat same-named indices from different sensors as identical measurements.
  • Check spatial and temporal alignment before fusion.

8. Ground truth is also measured

Field biomass, chlorophyll, disease scores, and yield are themselves measured with error. The lightweight calibration helper assumes the reference is sufficiently precise for the intended use. If that assumption is not credible, use the broader measurement-error machinery or a custom hierarchical model.

Interpretation checklist

  • Describe sampling and laboratory error.
  • Do not use the phrase ground truth to imply perfect measurement.
  • Propagate reference uncertainty when it is material.

9. Spatial-support mismatch

A satellite pixel may contain several plots, while a UAV mosaic may contain thousands of pixels per plot. Fusion requires defining a common statistical support or explicitly modeling change of support. Simply joining by nearest coordinate can create misleading certainty.

Interpretation checklist

  • State the support of every source.
  • Aggregate or model support differences explicitly.
  • Check edge plots and mixed pixels.

10. Temporal alignment

Acquisition times may differ by hours or days. For fast-changing traits, nearest-date fusion may be scientifically unacceptable. The 1.3.0 model records time but does not automatically invent temporal interpolation for unmatched sensor acquisitions.

names(f)

Interpretation checklist

  • Set a defensible temporal matching window upstream.
  • Use the spatiotemporal layer when interpolation is part of the model.
  • Report asynchronous acquisitions.

11. Uncertainty after prediction

bayes_rs_uncertainty() converts posterior prediction draws into row-wise posterior SD, credible interval width, relative SD, and optional threshold probabilities. These summaries are designed for mapping and triage without discarding the underlying draws.

if (FALSE) {
  pred <- bayes_rs_predict(fit_f)
  unc <- bayes_rs_uncertainty(pred, threshold = 5, direction = "below")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Map uncertainty alongside the posterior mean.
  • Avoid interpreting relative SD near a response mean of zero without care.
  • Keep the full posterior for downstream decisions.

12. Uncertainty sources are different

Posterior uncertainty can reflect coefficient uncertainty, latent sensor values, spatial process uncertainty, temporal persistence, random effects, and observation noise. A single map of posterior SD combines these according to the fitted model but does not identify their individual contributions automatically.

Interpretation checklist

  • State which uncertainty sources the model includes.
  • Do not call omitted sources negligible without evidence.
  • Use sensitivity analysis for structural uncertainty.

13. Calibration transportability

A calibration obtained under one canopy architecture, cultivar set, illumination regime, or growth stage may not transport. External validation by campaign or environment is more informative than a high in-sample R-squared.

Interpretation checklist

  • Report external RMSE when available.
  • Check bias across the response range.
  • Recalibrate or model group differences when justified.

14. Model comparison for fusion

A multi-sensor model can be compared with simpler sensor-specific alternatives. Predictive improvement should be weighed against cost, availability, and robustness. A small predictive gain may not justify an expensive acquisition stream.

if (FALSE) {
  bayes_compare_models(fit_uav, fit_satellite, fit_fusion)
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Compare on the same held-out units.
  • Include operational cost in decision analyses when relevant.
  • Do not confuse predictive weights with posterior model probabilities.

15. Decision layer integration

Because 1.3.0 returns ordinary posterior predictions, they can feed the existing utility, regret, and value-of-information layer. For example, a scouting decision can depend on the posterior probability of stress and the cost of a false alarm.

if (FALSE) {
  risk <- bayes_rs_uncertainty(pred, threshold = stress_limit, direction = "below")
  # Translate probabilities into a transparent action/utility model.
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Define the action before calculating utility.
  • State costs and consequences.
  • Keep the remote-sensing model separate from the decision rule.

16. Recommended workflow

A defensible fusion analysis moves from calibrated and aligned measurements to a declared model, checks the measurement assumptions, fits the posterior, validates out of sample, and only then produces decision products.

f <- bayes_teaching_data("sensor_fusion")
des <- bayes_rs_fusion(f, "biomass", list(uav=c("uav_ndvi","height"), satellite="sat_ndvi"), x_coord="x", y_coord="y")
plan <- bayes_plan(des)
if (FALSE) {
  fit <- bayes_fit(des, engine="brms", compute=bayes_compute(backend="cmdstanr"))
  bayes_diagnose(fit)
  pred <- bayes_rs_predict(fit)
  unc <- bayes_rs_uncertainty(pred)
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Calibrate.
  • Align supports.
  • Declare uncertainty.
  • Fit and diagnose.
  • Validate.
  • Map or decide.

Reporting template

A concise methods paragraph should identify the sensor sources, calibration reference, spatial and temporal support, measurement-error assumptions, Bayesian model family, priors, engine, diagnostics, validation partition, prediction target, and uncertainty summary. If a sensor-error standard deviation is treated as known, its empirical or technical origin should be cited.

Calibration and fusion audit worksheet

A multi-sensor analysis should document the following items.

  1. Reference measurement method and uncertainty.
  2. Sensor platform and acquisition campaign.
  3. Calibration sample size and response range.
  4. Calibration groups, if any, and the reason for them.
  5. External validation strategy.
  6. Spatial support of each source.
  7. Temporal alignment rule between sources.
  8. Predictor uncertainty source and units.
  9. Whether predictor standard errors are treated as known.
  10. Correlation among sensor predictors.
  11. Priors used for latent predictor equations.
  12. Diagnostics for the joint model.
  13. Comparison with simpler single-sensor alternatives.
  14. Operational cost or availability constraints.
  15. Sensitivity to calibration and measurement-error assumptions.

These items help distinguish a statistically integrated sensor model from a simple concatenation of columns.

Final interpretation questions

  • Would conclusions change under a larger sensor-error standard deviation?
  • Does one sensor dominate prediction because of scale rather than information?
  • Are fusion benefits stable across sites or campaigns?
  • Does calibration bias increase at extreme reference values?
  • Is operational complexity justified by predictive or decision benefit?
  • Can the complete calibration and fusion workflow be reproduced from frozen inputs?
